bibl.title: The Origin of Adaptation in the Auditory Pathway of Locusts Is Specific to Cell Type and Function

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: where in a layered sensory pathway the adaptation seen in one neuron actually arises
span.quote: The net SFA observed in the intact sensory pathway will typically result from the sum of many processes occurring between the stimulus and the recording site, each of which transforms the representation of sensory information, reflecting a general design principle ( Laughlin, 1989 ; Baccus and Meister, 2004 ). Disentangling the respective contributions to SFA within a pathway is a difficult task, however.

span.label: how to separate the contribution of intrinsic from presynaptic adaptation mechanisms in a single cell
span.quote: To separate the contribution of different mechanisms, we recorded from the same cell during acoustic and intracellular current stimulation.

span.label: adaptation mechanisms differ greatly between interneurons of one pathway and follow the cell's role in information processing
span.quote: We conclude that the adaptation mechanisms differ greatly among interneurons within this sensory pathway and are a function of their role in information processing.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We conclude that the adaptation mechanisms differ greatly among interneurons within this sensory pathway and are a function of their role in information processing.

span.label: spike frequency adaptation
span.quote: Spike frequency adaptation (SFA), the decrease in neuronal response strength during prolonged stimulation, is a feature of virtually all sensory systems.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To separate the contribution of different mechanisms, we recorded from the same cell during acoustic and intracellular current stimulation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In AN2 each spike triggers a slowly decaying afterhyperpolarizing current; during a stimulus these afterhyperpolarizations accumulate, progressively lowering excitability and thereby producing the adaptation.
span.quote: In AN2, slowly decaying afterhyperpolarizations during stimulation accumulate over time and lead to an activity-dependent decrease in excitability.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In AN2 the responsible conductance is inferred to be a spike-triggered AHP- or M-type current rather than a network effect.
span.quote: This finding makes a spike-triggered, hyperpolarizing AHP- or M-type current the most likely mechanism behind SFA in AN2 ( Fig. 8 , 4 ) ( Baldissera et al., 1973 ; Baldissera and Gustafsson, 1974 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In BSN1 the hyperpolarization is not generated by the cell's own spikes but is imposed by presynaptic inhibitory input driving slow hyperpolarizing currents.
span.quote: Because these were not the result of spiking activity of the BSN1 ( Fig. 4 C ), they probably are imposed by inhibitory inputs leading to slow hyperpolarizing currents ( Fig. 8 , 3 ) (see also Weschke and Ronacher, 2008 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A functional design rule: when a neuron's computation depends on the balance of incoming excitation and inhibition, adaptation must sit in the neuron itself rather than in its inputs, so that the balance is preserved.
span.quote: if the computation performed by a sensory neuron relies on the ratio of incoming inhibition and excitation, the neuron itself should adapt and not the presynaptic input.

span.label: current injection bypasses everything upstream of the cell, so the difference between the two stimulation modes is what the pathway contributes
span.quote: During acoustic stimulation, the time course of SFA elicited by current stimulation is convolved with the kinetics of all adaptation processes peripheral to the cell, whereas in the current injection it is not. Thus, only if SFA under acoustic stimulation is dominated by intrinsic mechanisms of the cell, the time course and its intensity dependence should be similar under acoustic and current stimulation.

span.label: in BSN1 the hyperpolarisation is not caused by the cell's own spiking, so it is probably imposed by inhibitory inputs
span.quote: This pattern was apparent in BSN1, which adapted quickly with time constants <20 ms ( Fig. 3 C ). The strong SFA was accompanied by long-lasting hyperpolarizations ( Fig. 4 A ). Because these were not the result of spiking activity of the BSN1 ( Fig. 4 C ), they probably are imposed by inhibitory inputs leading to slow hyperpolarizing currents

span.label: in AN2 long-lasting spike-triggered afterhyperpolarisations accumulate, pointing to an AHP- or M-type current
span.quote: Third, SFA can be dominated by intrinsic properties, as observed in AN2. This cell revealed long-lasting spike-triggered afterhyperpolarizations that accumulate over time and lead to a long-lasting reduction in excitability ( Figs. 4 , 6 ). This finding makes a spike-triggered, hyperpolarizing AHP- or M-type current the most likely mechanism behind SFA in AN2

span.label: a strong enough intrinsic mechanism can overwrite the time course inherited from upstream, which is what AN2 does
span.quote: Notably, in AN2 SFA was stronger but slower than SFA seen in receptor neurons ( Fig. 3 C ) ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, intrinsic adaptation mechanisms may overwrite the time course of SFA in the upstream pathway, provided sufficient adaptation strength.

span.label: a design principle stated as a conditional: if a neuron's computation depends on the ratio of inhibition to excitation, the neuron itself should adapt rather than its inputs
span.quote: Thus, the AN2 may represent a third functional principle for the distribution of adaptation mechanisms: if the computation performed by a sensory neuron relies on the ratio of incoming inhibition and excitation, the neuron itself should adapt and not the presynaptic input.

span.label: in BSN1 adaptation via one input would carry over to a later stimulus arriving on another, mixing temporal and directional information
span.quote: Then, SFA to a stimulus via one input affects the response to subsequent stimulation via another input and will lead to a cross-interaction of temporal and directional information.

span.label: TN1 conclusions hold only up to a limited response range because current injection could not reach the high firing rates evoked acoustically.
span.quote: Thus, our conclusions for TN1 are strictly valid only for onset responses up to 150 Hz.

span.label: Linking cell-type-specific adaptation to temporal processing needs long-duration natural stimuli that were not used.
span.quote: However, to further link cell type-specific SFA to temporal processing in the respective neurons, experiments with long-duration natural stimuli are required.

span.label: Only the stimulus side eliciting the larger response was tested, so directional processing was not assessed.
span.quote: Because we tested stimuli from the side that elicited a larger response for each neuron, our present investigation of SFA was restricted to temporal processing.

span.label: AN2 could not be analysed at the higher reference onset response because only one cell reached it.
span.quote: We did not analyze the AN2 at the higher onset response, because only one of the cells under study responded with >140 Hz at both stimulation modes.

span.label: Large propagated errors prevented interpreting the relation between acoustic and current adaptation ratios in AN2.
span.quote: At these levels the large errors rule out an interpretation of the relation between these two.

span.label: conclusions for TN1 hold only up to 150 Hz onset response, because current injection could not reach the responses that loud sound could
span.quote: In TN1, large sound intensities elicit very strong responses not reached by current stimulation, probably due to a more axonal position of the electrode in TN1 recordings (supplemental Fig. 1 A , available at www.jneurosci.org as supplemental material). Thus, our conclusions for TN1 are strictly valid only for onset responses up to 150 Hz.

span.label: AN2 was not analysed at the higher onset response because only one cell reached it under both modes
span.quote: We did not analyze the AN2 at the higher onset response, because only one of the cells under study responded with >140 Hz at both stimulation modes.

span.label: stimuli were tested from the side that elicited a larger response for each neuron, so the investigation of SFA was restricted to temporal processing
span.quote: Because we tested stimuli from the side that elicited a larger response for each neuron, our present investigation of SFA was restricted to temporal processing.

span.label: linking the cell-specific adaptation to temporal processing would need long-duration natural stimuli
span.quote: However, to further link cell type-specific SFA to temporal processing in the respective neurons, experiments with long-duration natural stimuli are required.

span.label: a predicted correlation between adaptation under the two modes was absent in TN1, possibly masked by propagated errors
span.quote: Cells exhibiting stronger SFA under current stimulation should also adapt more strongly to acoustic stimuli, yet no positive correlation between the ratios for acoustic and current stimuli was found for TN1 ( r = 0.09, p = 0.81) ( Fig. 2 B , C ). The putative correlation may have been masked by the large errors in the input–response curves that propagated to the adaptation ratios.

span.label: the gain function and a high-pass cutoff predicted from a time constant, applied to spike trains
span.quote: The high-pass characteristic, however, can be predicted by time constants of SFA. If onset and steady-state response curves were approximated by linear functions, the cutoff frequency f hi for transmission of AM stimuli depended only on the time constant of SFA τ and can be predicted by f hi (τ) = (2πτ) −1

span.label: propagation of error by partial differentiation, carried through an interpolation into the reported ratios
span.quote: Propagated errors were calculated by partial differentiation for all four spike frequencies contributing to the interpolation equation.

span.label: spontaneous activity in the same three cells analysed BEFORE AND AFTER the current or acoustic stimulation
span.quote: As a control, we analyzed the spontaneous activity in the three cells before and after current or acoustic stimulation.

span.label: adaptation measured under CURRENT injection and under SOUND are two different quantities on purpose: the first excludes everything upstream of the electrode, the second includes it, and the paper's whole result is their difference
span.quote: During acoustic stimulation, the time course of SFA elicited by current stimulation is convolved with the kinetics of all adaptation processes peripheral to the cell, whereas in the current injection it is not. Thus, only if SFA under acoustic stimulation is dominated by intrinsic mechanisms of the cell, the time course and its intensity dependence should be similar under acoustic and current stimulation.

span.label: the adaptation ratio is defined at a FIXED onset response (70 or 140 Hz) reached by interpolation, because adaptation depends on intensity and the two stimulation modes cannot otherwise be compared
span.quote: The comparison of SFA under the two stimulation modes is complicated by the fact that SFA depends on signal intensity. For this reason, we linearly interpolated the onset and steady state input response curves to obtain values for f̄ ss at a given reference onset response f on ref of 70 and 140 Hz, respectively. For this purpose, we took the first value of f̄ on ( I ) that exceeded f on ref and the value at the next lower intensity. By linear interpolation we obtain I ref , for which f ss ( I ref ) can be calculated by linear interpolation. The adaptation ratio r a is then given by

span.label: an adaptation time constant enters the analysis only where a single exponential already fits with r>0.8, so the reported constants describe the subset of responses that are exponential at all
span.quote: For the comparison of the time course of SFA under current and acoustic stimulation (see Fig. 3 ), only values of τ adapt ( I ) were taken at which the regression coefficient between fitted and real data was >0.8.

span.label: the three cell types are not a sample from a population but one identified neuron each per animal, named by morphology after staining
span.quote: Recordings presented here were obtained from 18 cells of three distinct cell types (TN1, n = 9; BSN1, n = 5; AN2, n = 4).

span.label: the three layers are feedforward with no within-layer connections, which is what licenses reading the three cells as three processing levels
span.quote: On present evidence there is no direct connection between the three cell types presented here. Overall connectivity in the network appears to be low ( Vogel and Ronacher, 2007 ), consisting of feedforward connections between the layers but no connections between neurons of the same layer

span.label: replicates → Weschke and Ronacher (2008)
span.quote: Weschke and Ronacher (2008) also found a high-pass characteristic in BSN1 with a cutoff between 10 and 20 Hz, which matches our findings ( Fig. 7 C ).

span.label: builds-on → Benda (2002)
span.quote: Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ).

span.label: replicates → Prinz and Ronacher (2002); Wohlgemuth and Ronacher (2007); Weschke and Ronacher (2008)
span.quote: Whereas the high-pass characteristics as reported here are difficult to compare with previous studies due to the different methods of quantification, the low-pass characteristics predicted by mean frequency confirm known cutoff frequencies ( Prinz and Ronacher, 2002 ; Wohlgemuth and Ronacher, 2007 ; Weschke and Ronacher, 2008 ).

span.label: extends → the finding that spike frequency adaptation is distributed across levels in vertebrate visual, somatosensory and auditory systems
span.quote: Our major finding is that spike frequency adaptation acts at all levels of a sensory pathway.

span.label: confirms → Weschke and Ronacher's high-pass characteristic for BSN1 with a cutoff between 10 and 20 Hz
span.quote: In TN1, the gain decreased for frequencies <3 Hz, whereas the prediction by a mean adaptation time constant of 60.0 ms lied at 2.6 Hz ( Fig. 7 B ). For the BSN1, which adapted much more rapidly under acoustic stimulation (mean τ = 18.7 ms), we observed a higher high-pass cutoff at 10 Hz (predicted: 8.5 Hz). The gain function of the AN2, which adapted slowly with a mean time constant of 143.6 ms, revealed a high-pass characteristic with a cutoff between 1 and 2 Hz (prediction: 1.1 Hz).

span.label: builds-on → Benda's measurement that locust receptor cells adapt to about half their onset response
span.quote: If adaptation mechanisms intrinsic to receptors and interneurons added up linearly, the ratio for acoustic stimuli r a ac in an interneuron that is monosynaptically connected to receptors should be the product of the adaptation ratio of the interneuron r a cu and that of the receptor cells. Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, in the simplest case: r a ac = 0.5 × r a cu . Our data were compared with this relation.

span.label: qualifies → studies that infer adaptation mechanisms from current stimulation in vitro or sensory stimulation in vivo alone
span.quote: So far, SFA has mainly been studied either by using sensory stimulation in vivo or current stimuli in vitro . In the latter case, intrinsic properties of isolated cells or small circuits are isolated, whereas sensory stimulation invokes adaptation mechanisms within the entire pathway.

span.label: current stimulation —contrasted-with→ acoustic stimulation
span.quote: During acoustic stimulation, the time course of SFA elicited by current stimulation is convolved with the kinetics of all adaptation processes peripheral to the cell, whereas in the current injection it is not. Thus, only if SFA under acoustic stimulation is dominated by intrinsic mechanisms of the cell, the time course and its intensity dependence should be similar under acoustic and current stimulation.

span.label: current stimulation —operationalised-as→ SFA
span.quote: During acoustic stimulation, the time course of SFA elicited by current stimulation is convolved with the kinetics of all adaptation processes peripheral to the cell, whereas in the current injection it is not. Thus, only if SFA under acoustic stimulation is dominated by intrinsic mechanisms of the cell, the time course and its intensity dependence should be similar under acoustic and current stimulation.

span.label: adaptation ratio —operationalised-as→ SFA
span.quote: The comparison of SFA under the two stimulation modes is complicated by the fact that SFA depends on signal intensity. For this reason, we linearly interpolated the onset and steady state input response curves to obtain values for f̄ ss at a given reference onset response f on ref of 70 and 140 Hz, respectively. For this purpose, we took the first value of f̄ on ( I ) that exceeded f on ref and the value at the next lower intensity. By linear interpolation we obtain I ref , for which f ss ( I ref ) can be calculated by linear interpolation. The adaptation ratio r a is then given by

span.label: RETRACTED (A CONDITIONAL MODEL PREDICTION, AND THE CUE WAS A MATHEMATICAL PRODUCT) · receptor —causes→ adaptation ratio
span.quote: If adaptation mechanisms intrinsic to receptors and interneurons added up linearly, the ratio for acoustic stimuli r a ac in an interneuron that is monosynaptically connected to receptors should be the product of the adaptation ratio of the interneuron r a cu and that of the receptor cells. Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, in the simplest case: r a ac = 0.5 × r a cu . Our data were compared with this relation.

span.label: TN1 —part-of→ receptor
span.quote: The auditory pathway of locusts at the level of the metathoracic ganglion is a hierarchical network with three layers: receptors and receptor-like interneurons, local neurons, and ascending neurons. We selected three exemplary interneurons from each processing level: TN1 receives monosynaptic input from receptor cells and exhibits spiking responses that are similar to those of the receptors, BSN1 is a local interneuron that represents an intermediate processing level, and AN2 is an ascending interneuron that transmits information directly to the insect's brain

span.label: BSN1 —causes→ inhibitory inputs
span.quote: This pattern was apparent in BSN1, which adapted quickly with time constants <20 ms ( Fig. 3 C ). The strong SFA was accompanied by long-lasting hyperpolarizations ( Fig. 4 A ). Because these were not the result of spiking activity of the BSN1 ( Fig. 4 C ), they probably are imposed by inhibitory inputs leading to slow hyperpolarizing currents

span.label: AN2 —causes→ afterhyperpolarization
span.quote: Third, SFA can be dominated by intrinsic properties, as observed in AN2. This cell revealed long-lasting spike-triggered afterhyperpolarizations that accumulate over time and lead to a long-lasting reduction in excitability ( Figs. 4 , 6 ). This finding makes a spike-triggered, hyperpolarizing AHP- or M-type current the most likely mechanism behind SFA in AN2

span.label: afterhyperpolarization —operationalised-as→ time constant
span.quote: Notably for the AN2, the time constant of the decay of afterhyperpolarizations resembled that of SFA in this cell type

span.label: spike initiating zone —distinct-from→ afterhyperpolarization
span.quote: Although the pronounced afterhyperpolarizations observed in AN2 provide strong evidence for spike activated adaptation currents within AN2 for both stimulation modes, the absence of long-lasting hyperpolarizations in TN1 and BSN1 after current stimulation could also be due to a site of recording distant from the spike initiating zone.

span.label: spontaneous activity —distinct-from→ recording site
span.quote: As a control, we analyzed the spontaneous activity in the three cells before and after current or acoustic stimulation. In this case, only spike numbers are evaluated, on which the actual recording site should not have an effect.

span.label: spontaneous activity —operationalised-as→ BSN1
span.quote: BSN1, however, remained less excitable and showed less spontaneous activity after the end of acoustic stimulation ( Fig. 5 B ) ( r = −0.95, p = 0.0003). Under current stimulation, there was no observable effect ( r = −0.39, p = 0.34) in any of the 5 cells tested ( Fig. 5 D ). This implied that BSN1, even though it adapted slightly under current stimulation, did not change its excitability on longer time scales; the strong effects under acoustic stimulation must have their origin earlier in the sensory pathway.

span.label: time constant —operationalised-as→ high-pass
span.quote: The high-pass characteristic, however, can be predicted by time constants of SFA. If onset and steady-state response curves were approximated by linear functions, the cutoff frequency f hi for transmission of AM stimuli depended only on the time constant of SFA τ and can be predicted by f hi (τ) = (2πτ) −1

span.label: low-pass —contrasted-with→ high-pass
span.quote: The mean spike frequency response of the neurons predicted the low-pass cutoff, as indicated by the circles in Figure 7 B . This dependence was apparent for the two different functions depicted for a TN1 ( Fig. 7 B , gray circles) which differed in the mean amplitude of the stimulus and consequently in the mean response. Although the high-pass filter characteristic and the general course of the function <15 Hz were very similar for both intensity levels, the cutoff frequency of the low-pass differed between the two recordings and depended on the mean spiking response of the cell.

span.label: RAM —operationalised-as→ gain function
span.quote: To describe coding properties, we presented RAM stimuli that elicited an onset response of ∼250 ± 5 Hz. RAM stimuli were filled with the same carrier frequency as the test pulses presented for the characterization of SFA. To obtain an estimate of the frequency transmission properties of the cell types, the gain functions were calculated.

span.label: BSN1 —contrasted-with→ AN2
span.quote: In summary, TN1 and BSN1 showed very similar adaptation characteristics when stimulated with current and revealed a moderate and linear SFA with time constants ∼50 ms. When stimulated acoustically, this pattern changed dramatically in BSN1 and became much more similar to the pattern observed for the AN2 that exhibited strong SFA with a high dependence on the stimulus level. In AN2, current and acoustic stimuli led to very similar results with respect to time course and magnitude of SFA. These findings provide evidence for strong network effects on SFA under acoustic stimulation in BSN1, whereas in AN2 SFA can be understood mainly by intrinsic properties. In TN1, SFA observed under acoustic stimulation is in good agreement with a linear combination of adaptation mechanisms within receptors and in the interneuron itself.

span.label: TN1 —contrasted-with→ BSN1
span.quote: In summary, TN1 and BSN1 showed very similar adaptation characteristics when stimulated with current and revealed a moderate and linear SFA with time constants ∼50 ms. When stimulated acoustically, this pattern changed dramatically in BSN1 and became much more similar to the pattern observed for the AN2 that exhibited strong SFA with a high dependence on the stimulus level. In AN2, current and acoustic stimuli led to very similar results with respect to time course and magnitude of SFA. These findings provide evidence for strong network effects on SFA under acoustic stimulation in BSN1, whereas in AN2 SFA can be understood mainly by intrinsic properties. In TN1, SFA observed under acoustic stimulation is in good agreement with a linear combination of adaptation mechanisms within receptors and in the interneuron itself.

span.label: encoder adaptation —part-of→ receptor
span.quote: Adaptation time constants for both stimulation modes ( Fig. 3 C ) were similar to those found in receptor cells (10–80 ms) ( Benda, 2002 ) in which SFA arises mainly from encoder adaptation

span.label: metathoracic ganglion —part-of→ AN2
span.quote: The auditory pathway of locusts at the level of the metathoracic ganglion is a hierarchical network with three layers: receptors and receptor-like interneurons, local neurons, and ascending neurons. We selected three exemplary interneurons from each processing level: TN1 receives monosynaptic input from receptor cells and exhibits spiking responses that are similar to those of the receptors, BSN1 is a local interneuron that represents an intermediate processing level, and AN2 is an ascending interneuron that transmits information directly to the insect's brain

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: In TN1, the time courses for acoustic and current stimuli were rather similar ( Fig. 3 A , B ) and did not differ significantly ( p = 0.37, Wilcoxon ranks sum test; acoustic stimulation: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; current stimuli: 49.3 ± 21.6 ms) ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Both current and acoustic stimulation revealed time constants longer than 100 ms and were not significantly different from each other (acoustic: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms, current: 123.8 ± 35.0 ms, p = 0.68) ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: correlation coefficient
span.quote: This is reflected in the correlations between the response strength during and the level of the membrane potential after stimulation ( Fig. 4 A , C ) (current: r = 0.04, p = 0.92, acoustic: r = −0.93, p = 0.0001).

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: E , Regression coefficients for linear fits to rate hyperpolarization versus maximal spike frequency for all recorded cells for current and acoustic stimulation.

span.label: nonlinear (exponential) curve fitting with model comparison
span.term: nonlinear (exponential) curve fitting with model comparison
span.quote: We verified that double exponential fits did not significantly improve the fit quality.

span.label: goodness-of-fit threshold for inclusion
span.quote: For the following analysis only data were included for which a single exponential fit yielded a regression coefficient >0.8.

span.label: mean and standard deviation
span.quote: Mean values and SDs for 10 repetitions are shown.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Each data point depicts the mean and SE mean of 10 repetitions.

span.label: propagation of error
span.quote: Propagated errors were calculated by partial differentiation for all four spike frequencies contributing to the interpolation equation.

span.label: linear interpolation
span.quote: Onset and steady state spike frequencies were derived from linear interpolations; error bars depict SD as calculated by propagation of error (see Materials and Methods).

span.label: spectral (gain function) analysis
span.quote: To obtain an estimate of the frequency transmission properties of the cell types, the gain functions were calculated.

span.label: Wilcoxon ranks sum test
span.quote: In TN1, the time courses for acoustic and current stimuli were rather similar ( Fig. 3 A , B ) and did not differ significantly ( p = 0.37, Wilcoxon ranks sum test; acoustic stimulation: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; current stimuli: 49.3 ± 21.6 ms) ( Fig. 3 C ). In BSN1 time constants differed between current and acoustic stimulation ( p < 0.01): current stimuli reduced spike frequency with a time constant of 49.8 ± 14.8 ms, similar to TN1, whereas acoustic stimuli led to shorter time constants of 18.7 ± 10.9 ms ( Fig. 3 C ). In AN2, SFA acted on longer time scales than in TN1 and BSN1. Both current and acoustic stimulation revealed time constants longer than 100 ms and were not significantly different from each other (acoustic: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms, current: 123.8 ± 35.0 ms, p = 0.68)

span.label: regression coefficient
span.quote: For the comparison of the time course of SFA under current and acoustic stimulation (see Fig. 3 ), only values of τ adapt ( I ) were taken at which the regression coefficient between fitted and real data was >0.8.

span.label: Three identified interneurons of the locust auditory pathway show three qualitatively different distributions of adaptation mechanisms: mixed intrinsic/presynaptic in TN1, inhibition-driven in BSN1, and intrinsic spike-triggered in AN2.
span.quote: (1) balanced influence of both intrinsic and presynaptic adaptation mechanisms in an interneuron that summates over several receptor afferents (TN1), (2) predominantly inhibiting input as the source for spike frequency adaptation in a cell that transmits both pattern representation and directional information (BSN1), (3) primarily intrinsic, spike-triggered adaptation currents within an interneuron coding exclusively for direction (AN2).

span.label: The time course of adaptation is cell-type specific, differing significantly between the three neuron types.
span.quote: The time courses of spike frequency adaptation differed significantly between the cells types.

span.label: Spike frequency adaptation is not confined to one station but operates at every level of the sensory pathway.
span.quote: Our major finding is that spike frequency adaptation acts at all levels of a sensory pathway.

span.label: The measured adaptation time constants successfully predicted each cell's high-pass cutoff frequency for amplitude-modulated signals.
span.quote: Using the adaptation time constants, we were able to predict signal transmission properties for the different cells.

span.label: All three interneurons behave as bandpass filters, with the low-pass edge set by mean firing rate and the high-pass edge by adaptation.
span.quote: All three neurons displayed bandpass characteristics ( Fig. 7 B ).

span.label: Which adaptation mechanism a neuron uses tracks the computation it performs, so the origin of adaptation is a function of the cell's processing role.
span.quote: We conclude that the adaptation mechanisms differ greatly among interneurons within this sensory pathway and are a function of their role in information processing.

span.label: three distinct distributions of adaptation mechanisms emerged across three cell types of one pathway
span.quote: By comparing current and acoustic stimulation, three distinct patterns of the distribution of adaptation mechanisms within the sensory network emerged: (1) balanced influence of both intrinsic and presynaptic adaptation mechanisms in an interneuron that summates over several receptor afferents (TN1), (2) predominantly inhibiting input as the source for spike frequency adaptation in a cell that transmits both pattern representation and directional information (BSN1), (3) primarily intrinsic, spike-triggered adaptation currents within an interneuron coding exclusively for direction (AN2).

span.label: AN ARITHMETIC NULL MODEL, NOT A DIRECTION: linear composition predicts the acoustic ratio equals 0.5 times the current ratio, and the data were compared against that line
span.quote: If adaptation mechanisms intrinsic to receptors and interneurons added up linearly, the ratio for acoustic stimuli r a ac in an interneuron that is monosynaptically connected to receptors should be the product of the adaptation ratio of the interneuron r a cu and that of the receptor cells. Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, in the simplest case: r a ac = 0.5 × r a cu . Our data were compared with this relation.

span.label: in TN1 the magnitude of SFA to acoustic stimuli was qualitatively in agreement with a linear combination of SFA in receptors and adaptation mechanisms within TN1
span.quote: Direct comparison of the adaptation ratios at 70 and 140 Hz ( Fig. 2 B , C ) showed that the magnitude of SFA to acoustic stimuli is qualitatively in agreement with a linear combination of SFA in receptors and adaptation mechanisms within TN1, leading to a multiplication of adaptation ratios.

span.label: A PREDICTED CORRELATION THAT FAILED: cells adapting more under current should adapt more under sound, and TN1 showed r = 0.09, p = 0.81
span.quote: Cells exhibiting stronger SFA under current stimulation should also adapt more strongly to acoustic stimuli, yet no positive correlation between the ratios for acoustic and current stimuli was found for TN1 ( r = 0.09, p = 0.81) ( Fig. 2 B , C ). The putative correlation may have been masked by the large errors in the input–response curves that propagated to the adaptation ratios.

span.label: BSN1 at 140 Hz adapted far more than the null model allows, implying processes the model does not contain
span.quote: At 140 Hz onset response, SFA during acoustic stimulation was much stronger than expected from adaptation mechanisms within receptors and BSN1 alone, suggesting additional processes underlying the SFA at higher acoustic stimulus levels.

span.label: AN ANALYSIS DECLINED AND SAID SO: AN2 was not analysed at the higher onset response because only one cell reached it under both modes
span.quote: We did not analyze the AN2 at the higher onset response, because only one of the cells under study responded with >140 Hz at both stimulation modes.

span.label: time constants were similar across modes in TN1 and in AN2, and differed in BSN1 where sound gave 18.7 ms against 49.8 ms for current
span.quote: In TN1, the time courses for acoustic and current stimuli were rather similar ( Fig. 3 A , B ) and did not differ significantly ( p = 0.37, Wilcoxon ranks sum test; acoustic stimulation: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; current stimuli: 49.3 ± 21.6 ms) ( Fig. 3 C ). In BSN1 time constants differed between current and acoustic stimulation ( p < 0.01): current stimuli reduced spike frequency with a time constant of 49.8 ± 14.8 ms, similar to TN1, whereas acoustic stimuli led to shorter time constants of 18.7 ± 10.9 ms ( Fig. 3 C ). In AN2, SFA acted on longer time scales than in TN1 and BSN1. Both current and acoustic stimulation revealed time constants longer than 100 ms and were not significantly different from each other (acoustic: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms, current: 123.8 ± 35.0 ms, p = 0.68)

span.label: TN1 and BSN1 showed very similar adaptation characteristics under current stimulation, this pattern changed dramatically in BSN1 under acoustic stimulation, and in AN2 the two modes gave very similar results
span.quote: In summary, TN1 and BSN1 showed very similar adaptation characteristics when stimulated with current and revealed a moderate and linear SFA with time constants ∼50 ms. When stimulated acoustically, this pattern changed dramatically in BSN1 and became much more similar to the pattern observed for the AN2 that exhibited strong SFA with a high dependence on the stimulus level. In AN2, current and acoustic stimuli led to very similar results with respect to time course and magnitude of SFA. These findings provide evidence for strong network effects on SFA under acoustic stimulation in BSN1, whereas in AN2 SFA can be understood mainly by intrinsic properties. In TN1, SFA observed under acoustic stimulation is in good agreement with a linear combination of adaptation mechanisms within receptors and in the interneuron itself.

span.label: THE TWO-SOURCE LOGIC: an intrinsic current would hyperpolarise after either stimulus, but only sound lets another neuron inhibit the cell
span.quote: A poststimulus hyperpolarization due to SFA can have two sources: if it is the result of intrinsic adaptation currents, then it should occur after both current and acoustic stimulation; however, only acoustic stimulation will cause another neuron to inhibit the observed cell, but not current injection.

span.label: in BSN1 hyperpolarisation tracked acoustic response strength at r = -0.93 and current stimulation had no effect at all
span.quote: Higher levels of acoustic stimulation led to larger hyperpolarizations in BSN1 ( Fig. 4 A ), whereas current stimulation in BSN1 had almost no effect on the membrane potential after stimulation ( Fig. 4 B ). This is reflected in the correlations between the response strength during and the level of the membrane potential after stimulation ( Fig. 4 A , C ) (current: r = 0.04, p = 0.92, acoustic: r = −0.93, p = 0.0001).

span.label: in AN2 hyperpolarisation tracked response strength under both modes, around r = -0.92
span.quote: In AN2, hyperpolarization under current and acoustic stimulation increased clearly with stimulus amplitude ( Fig. 4 A ) and correlated with response strength during stimulation ( Fig. 4 D ) (current: r = −0.92, p = 0.00001, acoustic: r = −0.93, p = 0.0003).

span.label: CONFOUND NAMED: an absent hyperpolarisation could mean the electrode was far from the spike initiating zone rather than that no current exists
span.quote: Although the pronounced afterhyperpolarizations observed in AN2 provide strong evidence for spike activated adaptation currents within AN2 for both stimulation modes, the absence of long-lasting hyperpolarizations in TN1 and BSN1 after current stimulation could also be due to a site of recording distant from the spike initiating zone.

span.label: CONFOUND ANSWERED BY CHANGING THE OBSERVABLE: spontaneous spike counts were used instead, since the recording site cannot affect them
span.quote: As a control, we analyzed the spontaneous activity in the three cells before and after current or acoustic stimulation. In this case, only spike numbers are evaluated, on which the actual recording site should not have an effect.

span.label: the spike-count control gave the same answer, and the two analyses agree
span.quote: Thus, the analysis of spontaneous activity after stimulation confirmed the results obtained by quantifying afterhyperpolarizations

span.label: A NUMERICAL CEILING ON THEIR OWN CLAIM: conclusions for TN1 are stated to be strictly valid only up to 150 Hz onset response
span.quote: In TN1, large sound intensities elicit very strong responses not reached by current stimulation, probably due to a more axonal position of the electrode in TN1 recordings (supplemental Fig. 1 A , available at www.jneurosci.org as supplemental material). Thus, our conclusions for TN1 are strictly valid only for onset responses up to 150 Hz.

span.label: afterhyperpolarisation decay differed between all three cell types: 5.6 ms in TN1, 24.6 ms in BSN1, 118.3 ms in AN2
span.quote: A fit by a single exponential function to the decay of afterhyperpolarizations showed that all three cell types differed from each other significantly at the 0.0001% significance level: 5.6 ± 0.7 ms in TN1, 24.6 ± 10.7 ms in BSN1 and 118.3 ± 34.7 ms in AN2

span.label: TWO INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENTS AGREEING: in AN2 the afterhyperpolarisation decay resembles the adaptation time constant
span.quote: Notably for the AN2, the time constant of the decay of afterhyperpolarizations resembled that of SFA in this cell type

span.label: the spike shapes explain the offset results: TN1 decays too fast to see, BSN1 has almost none so its hyperpolarisation must be extrinsic, AN2 accumulates
span.quote: The spike forms help to understand the result of the analysis of hyperpolarization at stimulus offset: in TN1 afterhyperpolarization decays so rapidly that no effect lasting for >10 ms can be observed. BSN1 displayed almost no afterhyperpolarization and thus only an extrinsic, inhibitory influence can be responsible for hyperpolarizations observed after acoustic stimulation. In AN2, slowly decaying afterhyperpolarizations during stimulation accumulate over time and lead to an activity-dependent decrease in excitability.

span.label: A CLOSED-FORM PREDICTION FROM AN INDEPENDENTLY MEASURED CONSTANT: the high-pass cutoff should be one over two-pi-tau
span.quote: The high-pass characteristic, however, can be predicted by time constants of SFA. If onset and steady-state response curves were approximated by linear functions, the cutoff frequency f hi for transmission of AM stimuli depended only on the time constant of SFA τ and can be predicted by f hi (τ) = (2πτ) −1

span.label: AND IT HELD FOR ALL THREE: in TN1 the gain decreased for frequencies <3 Hz where the prediction lied at 2.6 Hz, in BSN1 a higher cutoff at 10 Hz was observed with 8.5 predicted, and in AN2 a cutoff between 1 and 2 Hz with 1.1 predicted
span.quote: In TN1, the gain decreased for frequencies <3 Hz, whereas the prediction by a mean adaptation time constant of 60.0 ms lied at 2.6 Hz ( Fig. 7 B ). For the BSN1, which adapted much more rapidly under acoustic stimulation (mean τ = 18.7 ms), we observed a higher high-pass cutoff at 10 Hz (predicted: 8.5 Hz). The gain function of the AN2, which adapted slowly with a mean time constant of 143.6 ms, revealed a high-pass characteristic with a cutoff between 1 and 2 Hz (prediction: 1.1 Hz).

span.label: the low-pass cutoff is set instead by mean spike frequency, separable in one cell at two intensities
span.quote: The mean spike frequency response of the neurons predicted the low-pass cutoff, as indicated by the circles in Figure 7 B . This dependence was apparent for the two different functions depicted for a TN1 ( Fig. 7 B , gray circles) which differed in the mean amplitude of the stimulus and consequently in the mean response. Although the high-pass filter characteristic and the general course of the function <15 Hz were very similar for both intensity levels, the cutoff frequency of the low-pass differed between the two recordings and depended on the mean spiking response of the cell.

span.label: BSN1 and AN2 end up alike under sound while TN1 stays tonic and locks less selectively
span.quote: In summary, BSN1 and AN2 showed similar response characteristics under acoustic stimulation, shaped by a strong decrease of response strength over time. The TN1, however, responded tonically and showed stronger, but less selective locking to the time course of the stimulus.

span.label: and the BSN1-AN2 similarity DEVELOPS over seconds - it is absent in the first 100 ms
span.quote: Note that the similarity between BSN1 and AN2 developed over time only and was not observed during the first 100 ms

span.label: in AN2 adaptation is stronger but slower than in receptors, so an intrinsic mechanism can overwrite an inherited time course
span.quote: Notably, in AN2 SFA was stronger but slower than SFA seen in receptor neurons ( Fig. 3 C ) ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, intrinsic adaptation mechanisms may overwrite the time course of SFA in the upstream pathway, provided sufficient adaptation strength.

span.label: 18 cells in all: nine TN1, five BSN1, four AN2
span.quote: Recordings presented here were obtained from 18 cells of three distinct cell types (TN1, n = 9; BSN1, n = 5; AN2, n = 4).

span.label: MODEL ORDER CHECKED: double exponential fits did not significantly improve on single exponentials
span.quote: We verified that double exponential fits did not significantly improve the fit quality.

span.label: ERRORS PROPAGATED EXPLICITLY through the interpolation by partial differentiation
span.quote: Propagated errors were calculated by partial differentiation for all four spike frequencies contributing to the interpolation equation.

span.label: spike frequency adaptation (SFA)
span.quote: Spike frequency adaptation (SFA), the decrease in neuronal response strength during prolonged stimulation, is a feature of virtually all sensory systems.

span.label: rate coefficient (measure of post-stimulus change in spontaneous activity)
span.term: rate coefficient (measure of post-stimulus change in spontaneous activity)
span.quote: The decrease in spontaneous activity because of SFA was quantified by a rate coefficient:

span.label: sign convention of the rate coefficient
span.term: sign convention of the rate coefficient
span.quote: Negative values of this coefficient indicate a reduction of spontaneous activity due to stimulation.

span.label: SFA
span.quote: Spike frequency adaptation (SFA), the decrease in neuronal response strength during prolonged stimulation, is a feature of virtually all sensory systems.

span.label: adaptation ratio
span.quote: The comparison of SFA under the two stimulation modes is complicated by the fact that SFA depends on signal intensity. For this reason, we linearly interpolated the onset and steady state input response curves to obtain values for f̄ ss at a given reference onset response f on ref of 70 and 140 Hz, respectively. For this purpose, we took the first value of f̄ on ( I ) that exceeded f on ref and the value at the next lower intensity. By linear interpolation we obtain I ref , for which f ss ( I ref ) can be calculated by linear interpolation. The adaptation ratio r a is then given by

If onset and steady-state response curves were approximated by linear functions, the cutoff frequency f hi for transmission of AM stimuli depended only on the time constant of SFA τ and can be predicted by f hi (τ) = (2πτ) −1

span.label: stimulation mode (acoustic stimulation vs. intracellular current injection in the same cell)
span.term: stimulation mode (acoustic stimulation vs. intracellular current injection in the same cell)
span.quote: Each recorded cell was stimulated both acoustically and intracellularly by current injection.

span.label: stimulus intensity
span.quote: The time course of SFA proved to be strongly dependent on input intensity.

span.label: cell type (TN1, BSN1, AN2)
span.quote: For this study, we chose three different cell types with different response properties, namely TN1, BSN1 and AN2.

span.label: adaptation ratio (steady-state divided by onset spike frequency)
span.term: adaptation ratio (steady-state divided by onset spike frequency)
span.quote: To quantify and compare the magnitude of SFA, we computed the ratio between steady state and onset response at both stimulation modes.

span.label: post-stimulus membrane hyperpolarization
span.quote: Hyperpolarization was quantified as the minimum of the membrane potential within 200 ms after stimulus offset averaged over trials.

span.label: gain function / frequency transmission properties
span.quote: To obtain an estimate of the frequency transmission properties of the cell types, the gain functions were calculated.

span.label: recording temperature
span.quote: All experiments were performed at room temperature (22 ± 2°C).

span.label: onset spike frequency held equal across cells for the coding experiments
span.term: onset spike frequency held equal across cells for the coding experiments
span.quote: The intensity was chosen to elicit an onset spike frequency response of ∼250 Hz in each of the three cells.

span.label: adaptation ratio
span.quote: If adaptation mechanisms intrinsic to receptors and interneurons added up linearly, the ratio for acoustic stimuli r a ac in an interneuron that is monosynaptically connected to receptors should be the product of the adaptation ratio of the interneuron r a cu and that of the receptor cells. Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, in the simplest case: r a ac = 0.5 × r a cu . Our data were compared with this relation.

span.label: time constant
span.quote: The high-pass characteristic, however, can be predicted by time constants of SFA. If onset and steady-state response curves were approximated by linear functions, the cutoff frequency f hi for transmission of AM stimuli depended only on the time constant of SFA τ and can be predicted by f hi (τ) = (2πτ) −1

span.label: spontaneous activity
span.quote: As a control, we analyzed the spontaneous activity in the three cells before and after current or acoustic stimulation. In this case, only spike numbers are evaluated, on which the actual recording site should not have an effect.

span.label: 18 — number of adult locusts used in the experiments
span.quote: Experiments were performed on 18 adult locusts ( Locusta migratoria ), obtained from a commercial supplier.

span.label: TN1, n = 9; BSN1, n = 5; AN2, n = 4 — number of recorded cells of each of the three identified types (18 cells in total)
span.quote: Recordings presented here were obtained from 18 cells of three distinct cell types (TN1, n = 9; BSN1, n = 5; AN2, n = 4).

span.label: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; 49.3 ± 21.6 ms; p = 0.37 — TN1 adaptation time constants under acoustic and current stimulation, statistically indistinguishable
span.quote: In TN1, the time courses for acoustic and current stimuli were rather similar ( Fig. 3 A , B ) and did not differ significantly ( p = 0.37, Wilcoxon ranks sum test; acoustic stimulation: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; current stimuli: 49.3 ± 21.6 ms) ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: 49.8 ± 14.8 ms vs 18.7 ± 10.9 ms (p < 0.01) — BSN1 adaptation time constants for current versus acoustic stimulation, which do differ
span.quote: In BSN1 time constants differed between current and acoustic stimulation ( p < 0.01): current stimuli reduced spike frequency with a time constant of 49.8 ± 14.8 ms, similar to TN1, whereas acoustic stimuli led to shorter time constants of 18.7 ± 10.9 ms ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms; 123.8 ± 35.0 ms; p = 0.68 — AN2 adaptation time constants under acoustic and current stimulation, both slow and not different
span.quote: Both current and acoustic stimulation revealed time constants longer than 100 ms and were not significantly different from each other (acoustic: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms, current: 123.8 ± 35.0 ms, p = 0.68) ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: 5.6 ± 0.7 ms / 24.6 ± 10.7 ms / 118.3 ± 34.7 ms — decay time constants of the afterhyperpolarization in TN1, BSN1 and AN2, all significantly different
span.quote: A fit by a single exponential function to the decay of afterhyperpolarizations showed that all three cell types differed from each other significantly at the 0.0001% significance level: 5.6 ± 0.7 ms in TN1, 24.6 ± 10.7 ms in BSN1 and 118.3 ± 34.7 ms in AN2 ( Fig. 6 B ).

span.label: 2.9 ± 4.3% vs 14.8 ± 4.3% and 12.8 ± 1.5% — relative afterhyperpolarization magnitude in BSN1 compared with TN1 and AN2
span.quote: The relative magnitude of afterhyperpolarizations was significantly smaller in BSN1 (2.9 ± 4.3%) than in both TN1 (14.8 ± 4.3%) and AN2 (12.8 ± 1.5%), whereas no significant difference between AN2 and TN1 was observed ( Fig. 6 ).

span.label: r = 0.09, p = 0.81 — absence of correlation in TN1 between adaptation ratios under acoustic and under current stimulation
span.quote: yet no positive correlation between the ratios for acoustic and current stimuli was found for TN1 ( r = 0.09, p = 0.81) ( Fig. 2 B , C ).

span.label: current: r = 0.04, p = 0.92, acoustic: r = −0.93, p = 0.0001 — BSN1 correlation between response strength and post-stimulus membrane potential, present only for acoustic stimulation
span.quote: This is reflected in the correlations between the response strength during and the level of the membrane potential after stimulation ( Fig. 4 A , C ) (current: r = 0.04, p = 0.92, acoustic: r = −0.93, p = 0.0001).

span.label: <3 Hz observed vs 2.6 Hz predicted (τ = 60.0 ms) — TN1 high-pass cutoff of the gain function versus the cutoff predicted from its adaptation time constant
span.quote: In TN1, the gain decreased for frequencies <3 Hz, whereas the prediction by a mean adaptation time constant of 60.0 ms lied at 2.6 Hz ( Fig. 7 B ).

span.label: 10 Hz observed vs 8.5 Hz predicted (mean τ = 18.7 ms) — BSN1 high-pass cutoff versus the prediction from its faster adaptation time constant
span.quote: For the BSN1, which adapted much more rapidly under acoustic stimulation (mean τ = 18.7 ms), we observed a higher high-pass cutoff at 10 Hz (predicted: 8.5 Hz).

span.label: ∼0.5 — BSN1 adaptation ratio under current stimulation, constant across intensities
span.quote: In BSN1, SFA to current stimulation showed a constant ratio ∼0.5 ( Figs. 1 B , 2 A ).

span.label: 0.5 × r a cu — the linear-composition prediction the acoustic adaptation ratio is tested against
span.quote: If adaptation mechanisms intrinsic to receptors and interneurons added up linearly, the ratio for acoustic stimuli r a ac in an interneuron that is monosynaptically connected to receptors should be the product of the adaptation ratio of the interneuron r a cu and that of the receptor cells. Spike frequency in receptors adapts to ∼50% of their onset response ( Benda, 2002 ). Thus, in the simplest case: r a ac = 0.5 × r a cu . Our data were compared with this relation.

span.label: r = 0.09, p = 0.81 — the predicted cross-mode correlation in TN1, absent
span.quote: Cells exhibiting stronger SFA under current stimulation should also adapt more strongly to acoustic stimuli, yet no positive correlation between the ratios for acoustic and current stimuli was found for TN1 ( r = 0.09, p = 0.81) ( Fig. 2 B , C ). The putative correlation may have been masked by the large errors in the input–response curves that propagated to the adaptation ratios.

span.label: 18.7 ± 10.9 ms against 49.8 ± 14.8 ms — BSN1 adaptation time constant, acoustic against current
span.quote: In TN1, the time courses for acoustic and current stimuli were rather similar ( Fig. 3 A , B ) and did not differ significantly ( p = 0.37, Wilcoxon ranks sum test; acoustic stimulation: 60.0 ± 14.9 ms; current stimuli: 49.3 ± 21.6 ms) ( Fig. 3 C ). In BSN1 time constants differed between current and acoustic stimulation ( p < 0.01): current stimuli reduced spike frequency with a time constant of 49.8 ± 14.8 ms, similar to TN1, whereas acoustic stimuli led to shorter time constants of 18.7 ± 10.9 ms ( Fig. 3 C ). In AN2, SFA acted on longer time scales than in TN1 and BSN1. Both current and acoustic stimulation revealed time constants longer than 100 ms and were not significantly different from each other (acoustic: 143.6 ± 38.2 ms, current: 123.8 ± 35.0 ms, p = 0.68)

span.label: 5.6, 24.6 and 118.3 ms — afterhyperpolarisation decay in TN1, BSN1 and AN2
span.quote: A fit by a single exponential function to the decay of afterhyperpolarizations showed that all three cell types differed from each other significantly at the 0.0001% significance level: 5.6 ± 0.7 ms in TN1, 24.6 ± 10.7 ms in BSN1 and 118.3 ± 34.7 ms in AN2

span.label: 150 Hz — the onset response above which the TN1 conclusions are stated not to hold
span.quote: In TN1, large sound intensities elicit very strong responses not reached by current stimulation, probably due to a more axonal position of the electrode in TN1 recordings (supplemental Fig. 1 A , available at www.jneurosci.org as supplemental material). Thus, our conclusions for TN1 are strictly valid only for onset responses up to 150 Hz.
